title: A 60% win rate was below breakeven on this NQ strategy
author: person-person12
selftext:
I keep seeing win rate used as if it tells you whether a strategy is any good. The numbers from one NQ test show how much it leaves out.

I rebuilt the Powell 10am setup in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading), which I own, and ran the mechanical version from July 2023 to February 2026 on one NQ contract. It took 535 trades and won 60.2% of them. The average winner was $522 and the average loser was $806.

With that payoff, the strategy needed to win about **60.7% just to break even on those average outcomes**. It came in at 60.2%, finished with a 0.98 profit factor and lost $3,675. Half a percentage point separated the attractive headline from a negative result.

Its like a coin that lands heads six times out of ten, except tails costs more than heads pays. Counting how often you win hides the part that empties the account.

This was one mechanical interpretation of a discretionary setup, and historical results dont predict the next run. Win rate only becomes useful once the size of the winners and losers sits beside it.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The break-even win rate (loss divided by win plus loss) is the cleanest way to show this, and 60.7% against 60.2% makes the point well. One addition: with 535 trades, a half-point gap sits well inside the sampling noise, so I'd report the confidence interval on expectancy per trade ($7 loss per trade on a $600-plus swing) instead of treating it as a clear negative, and add commissions and slippage in a separate line. A 10am setup also depends on the morning's news flow, so splitting the 535 trades by scheduled-release mornings (CPI, FOMC, NFP) would show whether the result comes from a few event days. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for tagging them.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: You're right about the half-point gap. I'd use a block bootstrap on daily P&L rather than a plain trade-level interval, because adjacent trades can share the same regime. **The event split also needs bucket counts** beside net expectancy after fees and slippage, otherwise three CPI mornings can look like an entire market condition.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Agreed, a block bootstrap on daily P&L is the better interval, and bucket counts next to the net expectancy are what keep three CPI mornings from being read as a market condition. Pooling several release types (CPI, PPI, NFP) after checking that they behave alike would also give each bucket a more usable sample.
